summary: A row in a list of things a person can open — a badge, a title and a meta line, with an illustration cropped into the trailing corner.

figma.note: State=Default | Hover. The hover variant is the border colour and nothing else; the picture's rise has no Figma counterpart — docs/foundations/motion.md is the spec.

pairs.dont: Let the illustration answer the pointer itself inside a card.
pairs.do: Leave `interactive` alone and let the card pass `active`.
pairs.why: Two things listening to one pointer means the picture can play while the card is not highlighted, and a picture that responds reads as a control. The card is what opens; the picture answers the card.

pairs.dont: Start the drawing the instant the pointer touches the row.
pairs.do: Let the 120ms dwell do its job — a pointer crossing a list on its way somewhere else moves nothing.
pairs.why: A list is mostly crossed, not read. Firing on entry turns a scroll past six rows into six animations, which is the flicker that makes people turn motion off.

pairs.dont: Add a shadow or a raise on hover.
pairs.do: Change the border and leave the card where it is.
pairs.why: Rows sit a 2-gap apart, so a hover shadow lands on the card below — a visual artefact signalling something the border already says. Measured on Claude's own cards: border and background only, no movement at all. Not drawn: the wrong side needs a class the component refuses (a shadow, a wrapping title), and a mock-up would be a picture of something the library will not let you build.

pairs.dont: Let a long title wrap and push the row taller than its neighbours.
pairs.do: One line, truncated, with the full name available where the card opens.
pairs.why: A list is read by scanning down one edge. A row that grows breaks the rhythm the scan depends on, and the names that overflow are usually the ones that differ only at the end. Not drawn: the wrong side needs a class the component refuses (a shadow, a wrapping title), and a mock-up would be a picture of something the library will not let you build.

pairs.dont: Put status prose in the badge — "3 sites need attention".
pairs.do: Name the kind of thing this is — "Alert rule", "Fleet", "Report" — and put the count in the meta line.
pairs.why: The badge is how someone tells one row's type from another at a glance. A sentence there competes with the title and stops the column reading as a column.

pairs.dont: Choose an illustration because you like how it moves.
pairs.do: Choose it for what it depicts — a fleet of endpoints is `fleet-health`, a dependency run is `call-readiness`.
pairs.why: The mechanic follows the subject, not the other way round. A list where the picture does not match the thing teaches people the pictures are decoration, and then they stop looking at them.

pairs.dont: Give the illustration its own label as well as the title.
pairs.do: Leave the art `aria-hidden` — the card already has one accessible name.
pairs.why: A screen reader reading a row twice, once as a picture and once as a title, doubles the length of every list. The picture says nothing the title does not.

a11y: One target and one accessible name: the anchor, named by its title and meta line.
The art is aria-hidden and the drawing takes `label={null}`. Nothing is said only by the picture.
Focus turns the picture on immediately — there is nothing to settle, because arriving by keyboard is already deliberate.
The focus ring is the system's: 2px `ring/focused` with a 2px offset on the app surface, so it reads against both the card and the page.
Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the rise and the colour transition are both off; the drawing holds at rest and still says what it means.
